structure.title: Books I–II · How does a life acquire its shape?
structure.text: Aristotle asks what people seek for its own sake, then turns quickly to practice. A person acquires steadiness under danger partly by doing the things a steady person would do. This apparent circle gives a teacher and a city considerable power.

structure.title: Books III–VI · Whose deed was it?
structure.text: Choice, compulsion and ignorance introduce portraits of particular virtues. Questions about fair shares and good judgment then show how much depends on seeing what this occasion demands, even when a general rule is available.

structure.title: Books VII–X · Knowledge meets appetite, friendship and leisure
structure.text: People can see a better course and still take the worse. Pleasure and friendship complicate any picture of goodness as solitary self-command. The closing discussion of contemplation and education reopens the question of what life a city makes possible.

people.name: Eudaimonia
people.role: A life going well over time
people.text: Happiness here can be damaged by misfortune and judged across a lifetime. Translating the word as a passing feeling makes Aristotle's attention to friends, resources and repeated activity seem inexplicable.

people.name: Practical wisdom
people.role: Judgment in the case before you
people.text: The courageous response varies with danger, ability and purpose. Practical wisdom helps identify those features and deliberate well about action, a demand that remembering the names of virtues barely begins to meet.

people.name: The friend who wishes you well
people.role: Someone whose good can matter for its own sake
people.text: Friendship can begin because another person is useful or delightful to be with. Aristotle asks what happens to such a bond if the advantage or pleasure disappears. That case gives his longer account of friendship a practical test. What do I want for the other person when there is no particular reason for me to benefit?

context.title: The mean is relative to a situation
context.text: A trainer who gives every athlete the same ration may give one too much and another too little. The example explains why moderation need not mean choosing the amount halfway between two extremes.

notice.text: Look at what the good person enjoys.
notice.why: A generous gift made through gritted teeth can resemble one made gladly. Aristotle cares about the difference because an action leaves clues about the education of the desires that produced it.

notice.text: Keep the paired friends in view.
notice.why: Friends who want pleasure or advantage from each other can behave affectionately until circumstances change. The test is especially sharp when two people have understood the same friendship differently.

notice.text: Return to the sailors throwing cargo overboard.
notice.why: Nobody would choose to throw valuable goods into the sea on a quiet day. In a storm the person who could refuse may give the order himself. Aristotle uses the difference to prise apart the several things we can mean when we say someone had no choice.

opening: Someone can have money, admiration, and every pleasure available, and still have lived badly. Aristotle wants an account of a good life that can explain why. He examines the choices that become habits, the friends who shape judgment, and the uncomfortable gap between knowing what to do and doing it. His subject is the life a person actually practises over years, including what they enjoy, what makes them angry, and whether their apparent success has left them capable of using it well.
